questions.question_text:
A circle has circumference $43.96$ cm and diameter $14$ cm.
Use these measurements to find an approximate value for $\pi$, correct to $2$ decimal places.

options.why: Divided the circumference by the radius $7$ cm instead of by the diameter $14$ cm.
Divided the diameter by the circumference, inverting the ratio.

questions.question_text:
A circle has circumference $50.24$ cm and diameter $16$ cm.
Use these measurements to find an approximate value for $\pi$, correct to $2$ decimal places.

options.why: Divided the diameter by the circumference, inverting the ratio.
Divided by the radius $8$ cm instead of by the diameter $16$ cm.
Multiplied $50.24$ by $16$ instead of dividing the circumference by the diameter.

questions.question_text:
A circle has circumference $C$, diameter $d$ and radius $r$.
Which calculation gives $\pi$?

options.why: Inverted the ratio, dividing the diameter by the circumference to get $0.318\ldots$
Used the radius in place of the diameter, which gives $2\pi$ instead of $\pi$.
Multiplied the two measurements instead of dividing one by the other.

questions.solution_text:
$\pi$ is the constant ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.
$\pi = \frac{C}{d}$

questions.question_text:
Circle A has diameter $3$ cm and circle B has diameter $30$ cm.
How does $C \div d$ for circle B compare with $C \div d$ for circle A?

options.why: Assumed the ratio grows with the circle, because circle B is $10$ times as wide.
Assumed dividing by a larger diameter must make the ratio smaller.
Scaled the ratio by the square of the factor the diameter was multiplied by.

questions.solution_text:
Circle B has $10$ times the diameter, and also $10$ times the circumference.
The two factors of $10$ cancel in the division, so both circles give $\pi$.
It is the same.

questions.question_text: The distance around a circle is about how many times its diameter?

options.why: Compared the circumference with the radius instead of the diameter, which gives $2\pi$.
Treated $\pi$ as exactly $3$ rather than a little more than $3$.
Divided the diameter by the circumference instead of the circumference by the diameter.

questions.solution_text:
$C \div d = \pi = 3.14159\ldots$ for every circle.
The distance around is just over $3$ times the diameter.

questions.question_text:
Two circular objects were measured.
$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Object} & C\text{ (cm)} & d\text{ (cm)} \\ \hline A & 54.98 & 17.5 \\ B & 164.93 & 52.5 \end{array}$
Calculate $C \div d$ for each object, correct to $2$ decimal places. Which pair of results do you get?

options.why: Divided each diameter by its circumference, inverting both ratios.
Divided each circumference by half its diameter, using the radius instead.
Rounded each ratio to one decimal place instead of the requested two decimal places, then added a zero.

questions.solution_text:
A: $\frac{54.98}{17.5} = 3.141714\ldots \approx 3.14$
B: $\frac{164.93}{52.5} = 3.141523\ldots \approx 3.14$
Both measured ratios round to $3.14$.
